title: JANUARY 2026
overview: Journalism and Technology Trends and Predictions 2026 by Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism Nic Newman’s report examines how generative AI, answer engines, social platforms, and the creator economy are reshaping journalism and news publishing. Drawing on a survey of digital leaders and industry examples, it considers pressures on journalism, publisher strategy, newsroom AI, business models, and likely technology developments in 2026. A report on journalism and technology trends, drawing on a survey of digital leaders from 51 countries and territories and discussing predictions for 2026.
methods: Industry survey using a strategic sample of 280 digital leaders from 51 countries and territories; the report describes respondents as editors, CEOs, and digital executives.

Traffic data sourced from Chartbeat, including aggregated Google-search referrals to news sites; a report footnote says the referral data aggregate over 2,000 news websites and apps in the Chartbeat network.
Additional report input gathered through background conversations, interviews, and emails with publishers, academics, and industry experts.
key_findings: News-site referrals fell by 43% from Facebook and 46% from X over the previous two and a half years, according to the report’s Chartbeat data.

For 2026, publishers planned to put more effort into YouTube (+74 percentage points net), AI platforms (+61), and TikTok (+56), and less effort into X (−52), Facebook (−23), and old-style Google Search (−25).
Publishers were experimenting with Substack as a distribution channel and expanding vertical video, including a curated vertical-video feed in the New York Times app’s watch tab.
Publishers were more concerned about creators taking audience time and attention (70% somewhat or very concerned) than about losing talent to creators (39%).

Planned responses to the creator wave included making journalists more like creators (76%), partnering with creators for distribution (50%), hiring creators (31%), and creating a joint venture such as a creator studio (28%).

The report notes that building journalists’ independent profiles may help them leave with their audiences, citing Dave Jorgenson’s departure from the Washington Post and the subsequent collapse in reach of its Universe YouTube channel.
limitations: The industry survey draws on a strategic sample of 280 digital leaders from 51 countries and territories; reported question bases vary (for example, 264, 265, and 273).

The report cautions that audience concern about misinformation does not necessarily mean audiences will return to news media; many distrust news media or rely on comments and AI chatbots for fact-checking.
Fewer than 1% of news images or videos published globally include C2PA metadata; adoption requires ecosystem-wide buy-in, and metadata can be stripped out.
Platforms’ synthetic-content detection systems have been only partly effective; some experts suggest TikTok detects less than half of AI-generated content.
